newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Supervisors set out steps for cross-border vetting.
newsitem.headline: Supervisors set out steps for cross-border vetting.

text.p: Bank supervisors from some 140 countries have agreed to implement 29 steps to overcome barriers, such as banking secrecy, to effective cross-border supervision of multinational banking groups.

The proposals give supervisors tools to disect complex cross-border structures and gather information to help prevent such spectacular incidents as the 1971 collapse of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI).

The recommendations, which were issued on Monday, stem from a mass of practical problems that supervisors have encountered in seeking to carry out the Basle Committee's 1992 minimum standards for cross-border supervision.

These minimum standards built on the 1975 Basle Concordat principle that all international banks should be supervised by their home country authorities. However, the standards stopped short of recommending how supervisors should deal with the raft of practical problems they have confronted.
The 1995 collapse of British merchant bank Barings Plc highlighted the limitations faced by banking supervisors and the lack of clear rules for on-site inspectations.

The proposals were compiled by a group of members from the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision and the Offshore Group of Banking Supervisors. They were endorsed by the International Conference of Banking Supervisors (ICBS), which met in June in Stockholm.
Regional groups of banking supervisors will continue to track the implementation of the proposals and conduct a survey ahead of their next meeting in 1998.

The first set of problems identified by the working group concerns access to information as home country supervisors have experienced difficulties in getting all the information they need from host countries in order to do their work properly.
The paper recommends procedures for how to conduct cross-border on-site inspections by home-country supervisors.
The working group also tackles the issue of secrecy and concludes supervision supercedes banking secrecy.

"While recognising that there are legitimate reasons for protecting customer privacy, the working group believes that secrecy laws should not impede the ability of supervisors to ensure safety and soundness in the international banking system," the report said.
The working group therefore recommends that information passed on to other supervisors be treated in a strictly confidential manner and should only concern supervisory matters.

"If a host supervisor has good cause to doubt a home supervisor's ability to limit the use of information obtained in confidence solely for supervisory purposes, the host would retain the right not to provide such information," it added.
The working group also looks at so-called shell branches, a term used to describe financial institutions that set up a branch mainly as a front for fraudulent operations.

Home supervisors should be permitted to examine the books of shell branches wherever they are kept and in no case should access to these books be protected by secrecy requirments, the working group recommends.
The report also addresses the need to ensure that all cross-border banking operations are subject to effective home and host country supervision.

It recommends guidelines for determining the effectiveness of supervision, for monitoring standards in host countries and for dealing with corporate structures, which create potential supervisory gaps.
